name: Omar Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign. This conversation is confidential, including anything you wouldn't say at work. Could you describe a usual working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Omar, 27, and I lead a small electrical crew doing houses and business repairs. I have a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence, and I'm the one they call when a fault won't stay fixed. Today I found damp in a workshop junction box and had to explain why drying the lid wasn't a repair. I like getting work right the first time; I dislike finishing a day with another new office procedure to learn.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What should I understand about your household, money and way of working?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Leila, no children, and my own savings cover about three months of normal expenses. I earn the usual trade wage and there are some similar employers nearby, though I wouldn't resign until I had an offer. I never use AI tools; my paper test book has served me well, and I don't like unnecessary risks. I was brought up to learn a useful trade, honour your word and ask family before expecting strangers to carry you.

say: I'd say a **useful trade** still matters and welcome faster invoices without replacing my paper test book.
I'd rather hear a **customer's result** than another sales talk about new tools.
think: My **repair wage** looks secure, with three months of expenses saved and some similar employers nearby.
I can build an **ordinary life** without needing the world to change quickly around my work.
do: Keep leading **electrical repairs** and checking younger workers' tests now and through the first year.
Maintain the same **paper records** and normal household budget rather than buying new tools.
feel: **Calm** and relieved to settle into familiar work with a reasonable reserve behind him.
S0.quote: I don't need the world to change quickly to feel I'm getting somewhere.
fieldNote: His **resistance to tools** isn't an ultimatum against office software; he distinguishes his testing responsibility from other people's methods.
His **financial calm** rests on steady work, a moderate reserve and alternative employers, rather than unlimited savings.

steps.text: Keep leading electrical repairs and checking tests with the paper book

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a useful trade still looks like a useful trade. If the office can make an invoice faster, fine, but I won't be asking for a new screen to replace my test book. I'd rather hear the customer say the power stayed on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel my wage was secure enough to keep building an ordinary life. Three months of expenses won't last forever, but it's a decent reserve with steady repair work and a few employers around. I don't need the world to change quickly to feel I'm getting somewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd keep leading the repairs and checking the younger workers' tests. In the first year of that picture I'd keep the same paper records and normal household budget. I wouldn't buy a different set of tools because somebody else had a good sales talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with relief that I could settle into work I know well. I'd enjoy the weekend meal at my parents' house without another conversation about being left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a younger colleague praising an AI assistant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, show me the fault you found and how you proved the circuit was safe. That tells me more about an electrician than the tool used for the first guess. I can respect a colleague without wanting the same methods.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave if the office adopted AI anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I wouldn't leave over the office choosing software for invoices. I don't do those invoices myself. I'd draw the line at being told an unverified answer could replace an actual test.

say: I'd judge work by **safe wiring** and clear bills, while resisting pressure to turn every repair into a race.
I won't claim to know **software** I haven't used just because the office adopts it.
think: My **practical checks** should keep my own wage and hours steady over the next few years.
Faster booking could squeeze **travel and explanation** time and put office colleagues under direct pressure.
do: Log actual **travel and repair** times in the paper diary for one month now.
Continue familiar **repair methods** in the first year and use the diary to challenge impossible schedules.
feel: **Uneasy** about other people setting the pace, while expecting his own income to remain secure.
S1.quote: I wouldn't ask for a sacrifice before I knew there was an income problem.
fieldNote: He separates **irritation with scheduling** from an actual expectation of lost income and avoids inventing a household emergency.
His **response to change** relies on paper evidence and a direct conversation, without adopting AI or refusing all office change.

steps.text: Continue the familiar electrical repair methods through the first year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should judge each job by whether the wiring is right and the customer understands the bill. Let the office do what it wants with booking, but don't turn every repair into a race. I won't pretend I know software I haven't used.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own wage and hours should hold because most of my day is fault finding and practical checks. But faster bookings could squeeze the travel and explanation time out of the day. I'd be thinking about the office staff as well as whether the new schedule lets me finish properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd record actual travel and repair times in my paper diary for a month. During the first year I'd compare that with the booked day and ask the owner to correct impossible schedules. I'd keep doing repairs my usual way rather than start using AI because other people were enthusiastic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the pace being set somewhere else, but not expecting my income to shrink in the next few years. I wouldn't lose sleep over a quote-writing program. I would be irritated by a calendar that pretended a van could cross town in a minute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with an impossible appointment schedule?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show the last month's real journeys and say which appointment needed moving. If the owner still insisted, I'd ask for the instruction in writing and refuse to rush a safety check. I wouldn't try to hide the problem by skipping lunch every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change the household budget immediately?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Leila, my partner, that our normal budget still worked. I wouldn't ask for a sacrifice before I knew there was an income problem. We'd keep an eye on the schedule and wages, not start a household emergency over an office trial.

say: I'd separate **2028 planning changes** from hands-on robots around 2031, without claiming my licence stays valuable forever.
I'd remind the crew that **three more years** isn't a whole working life for younger electricians.
think: I expect **repair work** could become scarcer as the robot date approaches within the next few years.
At **29 in 2028**, I would need working income far beyond what three months of expenses can replace.
do: Cancel the planned **television replacement** now and retain the money for bills.
Ask the old training supervisor about posted **repair vacancies** nearby.
Apply after 2028 for those with written **pay and hours**, staying until a signed offer exists.
feel: **Anxious** about scarcer work, with a reserve and vacancy search providing some control.
S2.quote: Three months of expenses is a reserve, not a replacement for my trade.
fieldNote: His **belief threshold** is a real completed repair, not enthusiasm for demonstrations or an assumption that difficult work stays safe.
He preserves **household uncertainty** by refusing to count his partner's wages as automatic replacement income or assume a move.

steps.text: Cancel the planned television replacement and keep the money for bills
Apply after 2028 for posted repair vacancies with written pay and hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew I'm not persuaded that a licence becomes worthless in 2028 just because planning becomes cheap. The card puts hands-on robots around 2031, and I'd keep that difference clear. I'd also say three more years isn't the same as a whole working life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think work could become scarcer as that robot date approached, even if the first change only removed our paperwork. I'd be 29 in 2028, not somebody with retirement next door. Three months of expenses is a reserve, not a replacement for my trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd stop the plan to replace our working television and leave the money for bills. I'd ask my old training supervisor which nearby firms still had posted repair vacancies. In the first year after 2028 I'd apply to those with written hours and decent pay, but I'd stay here until I had a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and cross with myself for not knowing what work I'd trust next. I have a way to look, and I wouldn't be out of money tomorrow. But I wouldn't sleep as easily as in the slower disruption picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner that evening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Leila that I wasn't asking to move out of our home on a guess. We'd look at my actual pay and the reserve together before changing anything bigger than the television plan. I wouldn't count on her wages to replace mine without that conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What evidence would make you take the later robot threat seriously?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to see the robot doing a real repair, with the awkward access and testing included. That wouldn't make me rush to use AI; it would make me take the vacancy search more seriously. I can dislike a change and still believe what I see.

say: I'd keep earning and watch **actual results** rather than abandon familiar work immediately.
I'd remind younger workers that **robots around 2034** remain part of the same picture.
think: I expect **hands-on skill** to keep paying the bills over the next few years while I build a larger reserve.
At **32 in 2031**, I would still need earnings for a long time after the full thinking change.
do: Increase the **monthly savings** transfer within today's budget, first aiming for four months of bills.
Keep leading **repairs** rather than enroll in an unfamiliar career now.
Seek posted **service vacancies** after 2031 and apply only where written wages and hours improve.
feel: **Uneasy** about future change, while expecting continued work and wanting time to inspect actual opportunities.
S3.quote: I wouldn't enroll or pay a fee just to look willing.
fieldNote: His **resistance** persists over the longer timeline: he will inspect training terms but has not committed to taking a course.
The **savings target** depends on maintained wages, and he would reduce transfers rather than borrow to preserve an artificial target.

steps.text: Increase monthly savings within budget toward four months of bills
Keep leading repairs while investigating actual work opportunities
Apply after 2031 for posted service vacancies with better written terms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years means we don't have to throw away the way we work this afternoon. We can keep earning and watch actual results before making promises. I'd still want the younger workers to understand the robots follow around 2034, not disappear from the picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Compared with 2028, I'd expect more years of steady work and time to build a larger reserve. My hands-on skill should still pay the bills in the next few years. I'm not calling it a permanent answer, because I'd be only 32 when full thinking AI arrived.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd increase the monthly savings transfer by a small amount that our current budget can carry. I'd keep leading repairs rather than sign up for a new career I don't understand. In the first year after 2031 I'd ask the old supervisor about posted service vacancies and apply only where the written wage and hours were better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not rushing around as if I'd already lost my job. I would still dislike the idea of learning an entirely different way to work. More years would let me investigate a real vacancy before making that decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a job that required retraining?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask what the training actually involved before agreeing to it. I wouldn't enroll or pay a fee just to look willing. If it meant unpaid weeks, I'd need to see the actual offer and cost before choosing anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be the first savings target?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want four months of bills rather than three as a first target. If my wages dropped before I got there, I'd change the transfer instead of borrowing to say I'd saved. The point is a stronger household, not a number on a sheet.

say: I'd ask younger workers to learn **proper testing** while reminding myself to notice real changes.
I'd judge a **familiar method** by whether it still completes the job properly.
think: At **37 in 2036**, I would still need earnings when the later hands-on robots arrive.
My current **work and reserve** make the next few years manageable, with time to add savings.
do: Maintain the small **savings increase** while household wages allow it.
Compare paid hours and advertised **electrical jobs** on paper each year.
Apply after 2036 for better posted **repair work** if hours fall, keeping the job until an offer is signed.
feel: **Uneasy** about the longer future, with enough present security to continue ordinary household life.
S4.quote: The future wage on an optimistic graph isn't part of our household budget.
fieldNote: He rejects **assumed future income** and hasn't turned the discussion into an unmade decision about children or housing.
His **annual check** creates a trigger for an earlier job search while preserving his preference for familiar methods and low risk.

steps.text: Maintain the small savings increase while household wages allow it
Apply for better posted repair work if the current paid hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the younger workers to learn proper testing before chasing ten years of predictions. I'd tell myself not to use the extra years as an excuse to ignore actual changes. A familiar method still has to earn its place by doing the job properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 37 at the thinking change and about 40 when the hands-on robots followed in this picture. That's nowhere near an age when I could plan to stop earning. Still, my present work and three-month reserve make the next few years look manageable, with time to put more aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd keep the small increase in the savings transfer while our wages allowed it. I'd make a yearly paper comparison of our paid hours and advertised electrical jobs nearby. In the first year after 2036 I'd apply for a better posted repair role if the present firm's hours were falling, keeping the current job until an offer was signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the long future, but able to carry on without making every dinner a crisis meeting. I'd be glad of time to see what really happened to paid work. I wouldn't suddenly become the first person trying a new machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the decade lead you to change a family or housing plan now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I wouldn't tell you we'd decided anything about children or a different home today. I'd discuss any actual new commitment with Leila against the income we had then. The future wage on an optimistic graph isn't part of our household budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you keep familiarity from becoming a reason to do nothing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the yearly check I'd ask whether the same methods still got the jobs done and whether customers still paid for them. If hours were falling, I'd start applying sooner instead of waiting for 2036. I don't need to like the new direction before I look for a wage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 is the one that worries me most, because I'd still be a young tradesman with not much time to choose again. Actual paid apprenticeships for experienced workers changing trades would help, not just a list of courses with fees. I'd rather learn beside somebody doing paid work than buy a promise in a classroom.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask how a family talks about change before expecting everyone to be excited. My partner and I would need the wage, the hours and the cost of a choice laid out plainly. Being cautious about the household isn't the same as refusing to work.

headlineQuote: I'd rather learn beside somebody doing paid work than buy a promise in a classroom.
portrait: **Omar, 27**, leads electrical repairs with a technical diploma and master licence, using paper records and never AI tools.
He lives with **his partner**, has no children, earns typical trade pay and holds three months of expenses near some alternative employers.
His **traditional outlook** prizes trade skill, dependable work and household responsibility; familiar methods remain his first choice under change.
Fast hands-on competition makes him **anxious**; longer preparation supports conditional saving and cautious searches for real written job offers.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves a young tradesman too little time to choose another earning route.
whatWouldHelp: Actual **paid apprenticeships** for experienced workers changing trades would help more than fee-charging course lists.
